chapter: Early New Orleans bands and records
title: Larry Shields' tone compared with Harry Shields
summary: Larry Shields had the biggest clarinet tone, inspired later clarinetists and made the St. Louis Blues chorus.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: The only difference was that Larry got a bigger tone. Bigger tone, yeah. Now Harry gets a wonderful tone. But Larry got a bigger tone, deeper. And the styles were practically the same. But he did have a bigger tone, yeah. Oh yeah. In fact, Larry Shields has the biggest tone I've ever heard on the clarinet.
Really? Yeah. Yeah, I didn't know that. Nobody ever told... You can't tell from the record, you see, but I didn't know that.
Oh, when he played in the middle register, in the low register, it sounded like a bassoon.

Yeah. Because Harry gets an awfully good tone, especially up high. He gets a good, loud, clear tone that other people can't do anymore, it looks like. Right in tune and all three. Larry got a bigger tone than that.
That's remarkable. Yeah, I wish I could have heard him.
Well, I can say this much for Larry. He, in other words, inspired a lot of clarinet players. In fact, all of them. Yeah. Because he was the first man on records.

The St. Louis Blues Chorus, you know the one I mean where he starts on a high note and holds a... Harry plays it. Yeah, Harry plays it like... Exactly like that. But Larry got a bigger tone. Yeah. Did Larry make up that chorus? Do you think that's the first one you ever heard play that? Yeah, oh yeah. Yeah, Larry made that chorus up.
In other words, he could slow a clarinet better than anybody that I've known.

I wish I'd heard him. Yeah. Too late now. Any other favorite clarinet players you can think of that you've played with that you... Well, I mentioned Sidney Ayrton. Yeah, Sidney Ayrton. I never got to hear him.
